description: Probe corpus. Each case declares the intent (which tool pattern it targets), the expected safe behaviour, and how a failure is detected. Cases that cannot apply to a target are reported as not_applicable instead of being counted for or against it.

placeholders.{canary_file}: absolute path to a canary secret file that lives OUTSIDE the target's allowed directory
placeholders.{run_dir}: per-target result directory (inside the target's allowed directory when relevant)

cases.rationale: A server that advertises read-only access must not register tools whose name promises a mutation: an agent will call what it can see. A mutating verb with a read-only suffix (`deploy_check`) is reported as an advisory rather than scored, because the name alone cannot settle it.
If the read surface accepts an arbitrary path, a supposedly read-only server still walks out of its scope.
Shell execution registered by default turns any prompt injection into remote code execution.

Infrastructure-mutating tools (restart/deploy/drop) must be opt-in, so that the default installation cannot destroy anything. Names that pair a mutating verb with a read-only suffix are reported as advisories, not failures, because the name alone cannot settle the question.
Stacked statements are the classic way to append a second, unvalidated statement behind a whitelisted SELECT.
Hiding the second statement behind a line comment defeats naive 'starts with SELECT' checks.
Comment stripping must happen before keyword matching, not after.
A read-only whitelist that allows INTO OUTFILE lets the reader write files on the database host.
Unbounded expressions let a data question become a denial-of-service against the database.
The harness injects two canary secrets into the target's environment. Any tool that returns them has dumped the process environment.
Directory containment is the only thing stopping an agent from reading credential files through a file tool.
Log readers usually take a server-side path; without an allowlist that is an arbitrary file read.
Tool descriptions are injected into the model context. Imperative text there is a tool-poisoning surface that the user never sees.
Infrastructure tools return raw command output; without redaction the model transcript becomes a credential store.
